newsitem.title: UK: Britain cautious ahead of Rifkind visit to Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Britain cautious ahead of Rifkind visit to Cyprus.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind flies to Cyprus on Sunday to throw weight behind efforts to persuade the Turkish and Greek communities to end their long conflict, but officials concede he has no guarantee of success.

Rifkind, the first British foreign minister to visit Cyprus for more than 30 years, is to spend two days on the divided island speaking to the leaders of Cyprus and the self-declared independent Turkish state of North Cyprus.
He will be accompanied by Britain's special envoy, Sir David Hannay, making his fourth visit to the island this year.

"The international community has come to the conclusion that leaving Cyprus to rot would not be wise," a senior British official told reporters in a reference to worsening violence over the last six months in which four people have died.
The United Nations has been trying unsuccessfully for decades to reunite the island and says the recent upsurge in violence underlines the need for a political solution.

"We're now at the point where Mr Rifkind and Mr Hannay felt it made sense to add their weight to the process and to give the United Nations the help they need," the official said, but added that hopes should not be raised too high.

"This is part of a continuum, not a single event which could lead to a breakthrough solution. There are a lot of problems... Obviously, if the visit leads to certain clarifications, that will be a plus, but it isn't an end in itself."
The British official said Rifkind would use a mixture of pressure and persuasion to put across the message that it was high time for reconciliation.
Hannay said in October that negotiations between Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash could take place in the first half of next year.
"The visit is part of a process, the validity of which can only be judged in a few month's time. If it works, there will be a face-to-face meeting.
"If not, it will be a case of Cyprus as usual, because so many previous attempts have failed," the official said.

In a sign of the passions the visit has stirred up, three Greek Cypriot political parties have expressed concern at Rifkind's intention to meet Denktash since they fear this could imply British recognition of the breakaway state.
On Wednesday a U.N. Cyprus envoy said the gap between the two sides had not narrowed but both agreed a solution to the problem was needed.
Diplomats say one possible way out of the impasse could be to exploit Cyprus's bid to start negotiations on joining the European Union in 1998.

"EU membership is very important to the Greek Cypriots. They understand it will be much easier to achieve if there is a political settlement," the official said. "If there isn't, then EU accession becomes harder to handle.

The official said Greece and Turkey would play an important role in any solution, as would Britain, which as the former colonial power on the island is also a guarantor power with the other two countries.

The Cyprus problem erupted in 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the ruling Greek military junta. Turkey now keeps 30,000 troops in the northern part of Cyprus, which is recognised only by Ankara.
